passages.t: A gentle answer, and the LORD who sees
passages.happening:
The chapter opens with one of the book's best-known sayings: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (verse 1). ‘A soothing tongue is a tree of life, but a perverse tongue crushes the spirit’ (verse 4).

Over all of it is God. ‘The eyes of the LORD are in every place, observing the evil and the good’ (verse 3). ‘The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is His delight’ (verse 8). ‘The LORD detests the way of the wicked, but He loves those who pursue righteousness’ (verse 9).

The realm of the dead lies open before the LORD, and so, the saying argues, how much more the human heart (verse 11). And the mocker will not take correction: ‘A mocker does not love to be reproved, nor will he consult the wise’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This chapter closes the first half of Solomon's collection. Up to here most sayings have been contrasts joined by ‘but’. After this the forms become more varied, and the LORD and the king move to the center. Chapter 15 already leans that way: the LORD is named nine times.

Proverbs rarely mentions sacrifice and temple worship. When it does, it agrees with the prophets. Worship offered by people whose lives are unjust is detestable to God. Amos, Isaiah and Micah all said so, and Samuel before them.

Verse 11 names Sheol and Abaddon. Sheol was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a silent, shadowy place below the earth, and Abaddon, from a word meaning to perish, is a poetic name for it or for its deepest part. If even these hidden depths lie open before the LORD, the human heart certainly does.
passages.later: Samuel said it long before: ‘Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice’ (1 Samuel 15:22). And when King Rehoboam ‘answered the people harshly’ (1 Kings 12:13), he lost most of his kingdom, a harsh word stirring up anger on a national scale.
passages.hard:
Does God refuse to hear the prayers of some people (verses 8 and 29)?

These verses say the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, and that he is far from the wicked but hears the prayer of the righteous. Read with the rest of Scripture, their target is worship that tries to use God while refusing to turn from evil.

Isaiah heard the same message. God would not listen to the prayers of people whose hands were covered in blood (Isaiah 1:15). Yet in the same chapter he invited them to come and be made clean: ‘Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow’ (Isaiah 1:18). The wicked in Proverbs are those who keep on doing wrong, not those who cry out for mercy.

The Bible is full of sinners whose prayers God heard when they turned: King Manasseh in 2 Chronicles 33, and the city of Nineveh in Jonah. So these sayings do not describe a God who ignores anyone who turns back. They describe a God who cannot be bought with religious performance. No one is righteous enough to demand a hearing, and no one who turns to God in need is turned away.
passages.asks: A gentle answer can turn away anger. Ask where a harsh word of yours stirred up a quarrel this week, and what a gentle one would have done. And ask whether your worship and your daily life are telling the same story.

passages.t: Vegetables with love, and a timely word
passages.happening:
‘A joyful heart makes a cheerful countenance, but sorrow of the heart crushes the spirit’ (verse 13). ‘All the days of the oppressed are bad, but a cheerful heart has a continual feast’ (verse 15).

Then two ‘better’ sayings. ‘Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil’ (verse 16). “Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred” (verse 17).

‘A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger calms dispute’ (verse 18). ‘Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed’ (verse 22). A person takes joy in a fitting reply, and a timely word is good (verse 23). ‘The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may avoid going down to Sheol’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Verse 15 is honest about the oppressed. Their days are hard, and the book does not pretend otherwise.

The ‘better’ sayings set two good things side by side and choose the lesser one because of what comes with it. Most people in ancient Israel rarely ate meat. A stall-fed ox was food for kings (1 Kings 4:23). So choosing a plate of vegetables with love over a banquet with hatred would have been a striking choice to someone who seldom tasted beef.

Verse 23 is a small joy many people know: the right word, said at the right moment.
passages.later: The psalm agrees with verse 16: ‘Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked’ (Psalm 37:16). And James echoes verse 18: ‘Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger’ (James 1:19).
passages.asks: A table with love is better than a feast with hatred. Ask what your table at home is like, whatever is on it. And ask whether there is a quarrel you could calm by being slow to anger.

passages.t: The widow's boundary, and humility before honor
passages.happening:
‘The LORD tears down the house of the proud, but He protects the boundaries of the widow’ (verse 25). ‘He who is greedy for unjust gain brings trouble on his household, but he who hates bribes will live’ (verse 27).

‘The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked blurts out evil’ (verse 28). ‘The LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous’ (verse 29).

‘The light of the eyes cheers the heart, and good news nourishes the bones’ (verse 30). ‘He who listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise’ (verse 31). The chapter ends: “The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom, and humility comes before honor” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Verse 25 points to a real danger. A widow had no husband to defend the family's land at the city gate, and boundaries were marked with stones that could be quietly moved. The law cursed anyone who moved a neighbor's boundary marker, and the prophets condemned those who seized fields. Proverbs says the LORD himself guards the widow's boundary.

Verse 28 is a good rule for any conversation: think before you answer.

The last verse ties the fear of the LORD to humility. It is a hinge into chapter 16, which opens with sayings about God's rule over human plans. The line ‘humility comes before honor’ comes again in 18:12.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You must not move your neighbor’s boundary marker’ (Deuteronomy 19:14). And the psalm says of God, ‘He sustains the fatherless and the widow, but the ways of the wicked He frustrates’ (Psalm 146:9).
passages.asks: The LORD defends the widow's boundary. Ask who in your community has no one to speak for them, and what it would mean to stand beside them. And ask where you could practice humility this week, since the book says it comes before honor.
